beats.text: That conversation you keep replaying in your head? Here's what they actually thought.
You remember every awkward pause. Every weird thing you said.
Researchers paired strangers for a five minute chat. Then both answered two questions.
How much did you like them? And how much do you think they liked you?
On average, people were liked more than they thought.
Researchers call it the liking gap.
We're so busy judging ourselves that we miss the signs they're enjoying it.
Among new college roommates, the gap lasted for months.
So that conversation you keep replaying? They probably liked you more than you think.

sources: Boothby, Cooney, Sandstrom & Clark (2018). The liking gap in conversations: Do people like us more than we think? Psychological Science 29(11). Five studies; strangers' 5-min icebreaker chats: people underestimated how much partners liked them and enjoyed their company; also in longer chats, workshops (UK) and first-year suite mates (Yale, n=102), where the gap was significant Sept-Feb and gone by May.
APS press release, 10 Sept 2018: people are 'too wrapped up in their own worries' to notice partners' signals of liking (Clark).
